title: Lesson 10 · ADTs vs. Implementations
text: Lesson 10 · ADTs vs. Implementations An Abstract Data Type (ADT) is a theoretical model — it defines what operations exist and what they do, but not how they're built. List , Stack , and Queue are ADTs. An implementation is the concrete data structure that realizes an ADT — Array , ArrayList , and LinkedList . The same ADT can be built on different implementations, with different time complexities. Categorize — ADT or Implementation? (your quiz) Stack — choose — ADT (defines operations, not how) Implementation (a concrete structure) List — choose — ADT (defines operations, not how) Implementation (a concrete structure) Queue — choose — ADT (defines operations, not how) Implementation (a concrete structure) LinkedList — choose — ADT (defines operations, not how) Implementation (a concrete structure) ArrayList — choose — ADT (defines operations, not how) Implementation (a concrete structure) Check ADTs = Stack, List, Queue . Implementations = Array, ArrayList, LinkedList . (An interface is how we specify an ADT in Java — the L6 idea.) Multiple choice What does an ADT specify? The exact memory layout and code. The operations and what they do — but not their implementation. Only the time complexity. An ADT is the contract (operations + behavior). How it's stored and how fast each operation runs depends on the implementation you choose.

title: Lesson 10 · Implementing with LinkedList vs ArrayList
text: Lesson 10 · Implementing with LinkedList vs ArrayList You can build a Stack or Queue on either an ArrayList or a LinkedList. The choice affects the worst-case time complexity. A LinkedList adds/removes at the head in O(1) (just re-point _head ), and at the tail in O(1) too if the tail is tracked . LinkedList memory — True or False T / F LinkedList nodes are stored sequentially in memory. (your quiz) True False False — nodes are allocated piecemeal anywhere on the heap (non-contiguous) and chained by _next references. Arrays are the ones stored contiguously; that's why arrays get O(1) indexing and linked lists don't. Fill in The time complexity for adding and removing from the head of a LinkedList is Check Answer: O(1) . To add at the head you make a new node pointing to the old head and move _head ; to remove, you move _head to _head.next . No shifting, no walking — constant time. (This is exactly what a Stack needs.) The one you got wrong — worst-case comparison T / F For both Stacks and Queues, the LinkedList implementation has a better (worst case) time complexity than ArrayList. (your quiz — answer is True) True False True. LinkedList stack/queue operations are O(1) worst case (re-point head/tail). ArrayList is only O(1) amortized — its worst case is O(n) : a push may trigger a resize (copy the whole array), and dequeuing from the front of an ArrayList shifts every element. So for the guaranteed worst case, LinkedList wins. Multiple choice Why can an ArrayList push (add) be O(n) in the worst case? Because arrays can't hold objects. When the backing array is full, it must allocate a bigger array and copy every element over. Because ArrayList has no push method. That resize-and-copy is the O(n) worst case. It's rare (so amortized O(1)), but a LinkedList never needs it — its worst case stays O(1). This is the amortized-vs-worst-case distinction from Lesson 9. Why LinkedList for quick sort? Multiple choice The slides ask which list is best for quick sort. The key is which can swap elements efficiently. Which wins, and why? LinkedList — swapping is just re-pointing references (no shifting) ArrayList — because indexing is O(1) Neither can swap Slide 45: LinkedList , because a swap is a matter of re-pointing node references rather than moving data around in a fixed array. (Note the "sort on demand" bubble-sort example was O(n³) for both — the data structure doesn't always change the order.)

title: Lesson 10 · Code Writing
text: Lesson 10 · Code Writing Both are built on a linked list of nodes. A Stack uses the head for everything; a Queue uses the head to dequeue and a tracked tail to enqueue — both O(1). 1. A Stack on a linked list Write push , pop , and peek for a linked stack. Add and remove at the head so everything is O(1). { ... }"> Show solution public class LinkedStack <T> { private Node<T> _head; private int _size; public void push (T element) { // add at head — O(1) _head = new NodeImpl <>(element, _head); _size++; } public T pop () { // remove head — O(1) T v = _head.getValue(); _head = _head.getNext(); _size--; return v; } public T peek () { return _head.getValue(); } // look, don't remove } Because push and pop both work at the head — new node points to the old head; pop moves _head forward — there's no shifting or walking, so both are O(1) worst case. 2. A Queue on a linked list Write enqueue and dequeue . Enqueue at the tail (tracked) and dequeue from the head — both O(1). Handle the empty case. { ... }"> Show solution public class LinkedQueue <T> { private Node<T> _head, _tail; private int _size; public void enqueue (T element) { // add at tail — O(1) Node<T> n = new NodeImpl <>(element, null ); if (_tail == null ) { _head = n; _tail = n; } // was empty else { _tail.setNext(n); _tail = n; } _size++; } public T dequeue () { // remove head — O(1) T v = _head.getValue(); _head = _head.getNext(); if (_head == null ) _tail = null ; // became empty _size--; return v; } } The tracked _tail is what makes enqueue O(1) — without it you'd have to walk the whole list to reach the end (O(n)). Dequeue at the head is naturally O(1). Don't forget: when the last element leaves, reset _tail to null too.

title: Lesson 11 · Binary Trees
text: Lesson 11 · Binary Trees A tree is a non-linear data structure of nodes. A binary tree restricts each node to at most 2 children — a left and a right . The structure is recursive : each node is itself the root of a binary tree, so operations ( contains , height , …) are written recursively and can be called on the nodes directly — no separate "manager" class needed. Fill in — how many children Binary trees can have up to children. Check Answer: 2 (a left child and a right child). A node with 0 children is a leaf . Fill in — the fields of a tree node This is the quiz question — note the leading-underscore field convention it wanted. The fields of a binary tree node are , , , and . Check all Answers: _value , _left , _right , and _parent (references). The value, plus references to the left child, right child, and — so you can move up the tree — the parent. ("Value"/"Left Reference" without the underscore was marked wrong; the field convention uses _ .) Terminology Root — choose — The single top node — the whole tree hangs from it A node with no children (empty left and empty right) Number of edges from the root down to the deepest leaf A node directly above another (its child) Leaf — choose — The single top node — the whole tree hangs from it A node with no children (empty left and empty right) Number of edges from the root down to the deepest leaf A node directly above another (its child) Height — choose — The single top node — the whole tree hangs from it A node with no children (empty left and empty right) Number of edges from the root down to the deepest leaf A node directly above another (its child) Parent — choose — The single top node — the whole tree hangs from it A node with no children (empty left and empty right) Number of edges from the root down to the deepest leaf A node directly above another (its child) Check Height ↔ number of nodes For a binary tree of height h , the number of nodes n is between h + 1 (a straight "stick") and 2 h+1 − 1 (completely full). Flipping it: for n nodes, the height is between ⌊log₂(n+1)⌋ − 1 (balanced) and n − 1 (a stick). Multiple choice Which tree shape gives the smallest height for n nodes (and therefore the fastest search)? A "stick" — every node has one child (like a linked list) A balanced tree — each level filled before the next Height doesn't depend on shape A balanced tree packs n nodes into ~log₂ n levels, so its height is minimal. A stick degenerates to height n−1 — no better than a list.

text: Lesson 11 · Tree Traversals A traversal visits every node in some order. Depth-first (DFS) plunges down before backtracking; breadth-first (BFS) processes a whole level before going deeper. The three DFS orders differ only in when you process the node relative to recursing on its children. The three depth-first orders Pre-order — choose — Process the value, THEN recurse on children Recurse on the left, process the value, THEN recurse on the right Recurse on children, THEN process the value In-order — choose — Process the value, THEN recurse on children Recurse on the left, process the value, THEN recurse on the right Recurse on children, THEN process the value Post-order — choose — Process the value, THEN recurse on children Recurse on the left, process the value, THEN recurse on the right Recurse on children, THEN process the value Check ➡ Watch all four traversals run node-by-node with the stack/queue drawn in the Diagram It tab. Check both Answers: stack and queue (matches your quiz). DFS: push root, then loop — pop, process, push children (LIFO dives deep). BFS: enqueue root, then loop — dequeue, process, enqueue children (FIFO sweeps each level). Note: these are data-structure stacks/queues (which themselves live on the heap) — separate from the L4 stack/heap memory model. The tree's node objects always live on the heap. The n-ary in-order question from your quiz For the general tree in your quiz (nodes can have > 2 children), the rule is: recurse on the first half of the children (middle child counts as first half), process the value, then recurse on the rest. title: Lesson 11 · Binary Search Trees
text: Lesson 11 · Binary Search Trees A Binary Search Tree (BST) is a binary tree with an ordering invariant : for every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller , and all values in its right subtree are larger — and each subtree is itself a BST. Values must be comparable. Every BST is a binary tree, but not every binary tree is a BST. The invariants Multiple choice In a BST, where do you look for a value smaller than the current node? The right subtree The left subtree Either — order doesn't matter Left = smaller, right = larger. That single rule is what lets contains discard half the tree at each step (when balanced). T / F An in-order traversal of a BST visits the values in sorted order. True False True — in-order is "left, self, right," and in a BST left < self < right at every node, so the whole traversal comes out ascending. (Try it in Diagram It: in-order of the sample BST gives 2, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14.) Search cost depends on shape Slide 51 — same values, two insert orders, very different trees: insert(8, 5, 12, 2, 6, 10, 14) → balanced 8 / \\ 5 12 / \\ / \\ 2 6 10 14 contains(14) → O(log n) insert(2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14) → a "stick" 2 \\ 4 \\ 6 \\ 8 ... → 14 contains(14) → O(n) Multiple choice Why is contains(14) O(n) on the second tree? Because 14 isn't in the tree. Because BST search is always O(n). Inserting already-sorted values makes a one-sided "stick," so search must walk all n nodes — no halving happens. The BST's speed comes from halving, which needs a balanced shape. Inserting sorted data degenerates it into a linked list (height n−1), so search is O(n). You don't control the shape — it depends on insert order. The reassignment pattern for insert / remove Insert and remove may mutate the tree or return a new one , so they return the tree , and when you recurse on a child you must replace the child with the result : _left = _left.insert(element); or _right = _right.remove(x); Multiple choice You're removing value x from a BST. If x is greater than the current node's value, what is the next line? (Your quiz question.) _left.remove(x); _left = _left.remove(x); _right.remove(x); _right = _right.remove(x); _right = _right.remove(x); . Two things must be right: (1) x is greater → go right ; (2) you must reassign _right to the returned tree, or the change is lost. _right.remove(x); without the assignment throws away the result. Multiple choice Removing a node with two children is the tricky case. What's the standard fix? Delete the whole subtree. Find the min of the right subtree , copy it into this node, then remove that min from the right subtree. Swap the node with the root. Slide 49: replace the value with the smallest value in the right subtree (the next-largest overall), then recursively remove that min — which is guaranteed to be a leaf or have only a right child, i.e. an easy case.

title: Lesson 11 · Code Writing
text: Lesson 11 · Code Writing Trees are recursive, so most methods follow the shape: handle the base/empty case, then combine results from the left and right children. Write each, then reveal. 1. The tree node class Write BinaryTreeImpl<T> with private _value , _left , and _right (each a BinaryTree<T> ), a constructor taking all three, and getters/setters. implements BinaryTree { ... }"> Show solution public class BinaryTreeImpl <T> implements BinaryTree <T> { private T _value; private BinaryTree<T> _left; private BinaryTree<T> _right; public BinaryTreeImpl (T value, BinaryTree<T> left, BinaryTree<T> right) { _value = value; _left = left; _right = right; } public T getValue () { return _value; } public void setValue (T value) { _value = value; } public BinaryTree<T> getLeft () { return _left; } public void setLeft (BinaryTree<T> l) { _left = l; } public BinaryTree<T> getRight () { return _right; } public void setRight (BinaryTree<T> r) { _right = r; } } Just like a LinkedList node, but with two forward references ( _left , _right ) instead of one _next . That second branch is what makes it a tree. 2. height() Write height() — the number of edges from this node to its deepest leaf. A node with no children has height 0. ( null child = empty.) Show solution public int height () { if (_left == null && _right == null ) return 0 ; // leaf else if (_right == null ) return _left.height() + 1 ; else if (_left == null ) return _right.height() + 1 ; else return Math.max(_left.height(), _right.height()) + 1 ; } Recursive shape: a node's height is 1 + the taller of its two children's heights. The base case is a leaf (height 0). This is BinaryTreeImpl.height() from the L11 code. 3. contains() — plain binary tree Write contains(T value) for a general binary tree (no ordering) — it must search both sides. Show solution public boolean contains (T value) { if (value.equals(_value)) return true ; if (_left == null && _right == null ) return false ; if (_right == null ) return _left.contains(value); if (_left == null ) return _right.contains(value); return _left.contains(value) || _right.contains(value); // check BOTH } Because a plain binary tree has no ordering, you have to look left and right → O(n). The whole point of a BST is to replace this with a single-direction search. 4. contains() — BST version (uses ordering) Now write contains for a BST : compare, then recurse into only one side. Assume T is Comparable (use compareTo ). Show solution public boolean contains (T value) { int cmp = value.compareTo(_value); if (cmp == 0 ) return true ; // found it if (cmp < 0 ) // smaller → go left return _left != null && _left.contains(value); else // larger → go right return _right != null && _right.contains(value); } One comparison tells you which single side to search, so you throw away half the tree each step — O(log n) when balanced. That's the payoff of the BST invariant. 5. Recursive traversals (print) Write pre-, in-, and post-order print methods. Notice they differ by one line's position . Show solution public void preOrder () { System.out.print(_value + " " ); // value FIRST if (_left != null ) _left.preOrder(); if (_right != null ) _right.preOrder(); } public void inOrder () { if (_left != null ) _left.inOrder(); System.out.print(_value + " " ); // value in the MIDDLE if (_right != null ) _right.inOrder(); } public void postOrder () { if (_left != null ) _left.postOrder(); if (_right != null ) _right.postOrder(); System.out.print(_value + " " ); // value LAST } Same three lines every time — only the position of the "process value" line changes: first (pre), between the two recursions (in), or last (post). Note: this recursive version uses the JVM call stack instead of an explicit stack object — but it produces the exact same order.

The interface public interface PriorityQueue > { void enqueue (V value, P priority); V dequeue (); // removes and returns the MIN-priority value V getMin (); // peek the min without removing int size (); } Note the two generics: V = the value's type, P = the priority's type (must be Comparable so priorities can be ordered). The value with priority 3 (first enqueued) The value with priority -4 (the smallest) The value with priority 100 (the largest) -4 — a min-priority queue always removes the smallest priority first, regardless of insertion order. title: Lesson 12 · Binary Min Tree (BMT)
text: Lesson 12 · Binary Min Tree (BMT) A Binary Min Tree is one implementation of a priority queue: a balanced binary tree where every node's value is smaller than all values in both its subtrees. So the minimum is always at the root — getMin() is O(1). It stays balanced by always inserting into the shorter subtree. Fill in — the BMT invariant (your quiz) A BMT's value is than all values in both the left and right subtrees. Check Answer: smaller . Each node is the minimum of its whole subtree → the root is the global minimum. (This is the min-heap property : parent ≤ every descendant.) True or False — balance (your quiz) T / F BMTs are balanced binary trees. True False True. The enqueue logic inserts into whichever subtree is shorter ( if (_left.getHeight() <= _right.getHeight()) ), keeping the tree balanced — which keeps its height O(log n) and its operations fast. Multiple choice How does a BMT keep the minimum at the root during enqueue ? If the new value is smaller than the root, it swaps them, then pushes the larger old root down into a subtree. It sorts the whole tree after each insert. It puts the new value at a leaf and never moves it. From BinaryMinTree.enqueue : if the new priority is smaller than the root's, swap so the smaller stays on top, then recurse the larger one down into the shorter subtree. That "bubble the small one up / push the big one down" is the heart of a heap.

text: Lesson 12 · Binary Heap (array-based) A Binary Heap is the other implementation: a complete binary tree (every level full, last level filled left-to-right) stored compactly in an array — no node objects or pointers. A min-heap keeps parent ≤ children, so the min sits at index 0. The tree shape is implied by array index arithmetic . title: Lesson 12 · Code Writing — Array Heap
text: Lesson 12 · Code Writing — Array Heap An array min-heap needs three tiny index helpers, then insert (sift up) and removeMin (sift down). Assume the heap lives in int[] _data with _size elements. 1. Index helpers Write leftChild(int i) , rightChild(int i) , and parent(int i) . Show solution private int leftChild ( int i) { return 2 *i + 1 ; } private int rightChild ( int i) { return 2 *i + 2 ; } private int parent ( int i) { return (i - 1 ) / 2 ; } These three formulas are the tree structure — no node objects, no pointers. From index i you can reach its children and parent in O(1). 2. insert (sift up) Write insert(int value) : put it at the end, then swap it up while it's smaller than its parent. Show solution public void insert ( int value) { _data[_size] = value; // add at the end int i = _size; _size++; while (i > 0 && _data[i] < _data[ parent (i)]) { // sift up swap (i, parent (i)); i = parent (i); } } Add at the first free slot, then bubble it toward the root as long as it's smaller than its parent. It rises at most the tree's height → O(log n). 3. removeMin (sift down) Write removeMin() : save the root, move the last element to the root, then swap it down with its smaller child while it's larger. Show solution public int removeMin () { int min = _data[ 0 ]; _size--; _data[ 0 ] = _data[_size]; // last element to the root int i = 0 ; while ( leftChild (i) < _size) { // sift down int smaller = leftChild (i); int r = rightChild (i); if (r < _size && _data[r] < _data[smaller]) smaller = r; if (_data[i] <= _data[smaller]) break ; // heap property restored swap (i, smaller); i = smaller; } return min; } Take the root (the min), fill the hole with the last element, then push it down — always swapping toward the smaller child — until both children are ≥ it. O(log n).

title: Lesson 13 · AVL Tree Invariants
text: Lesson 13 · AVL Tree Invariants An AVL tree (Adelson-Velsky & Landis) is a self-balancing BST . Each node has a balance factor BF = H(left) − H(right) (difference in subtree heights). A tree is strictly balanced when every node has |BF| ≤ 1 . So an AVL tree is a BST that keeps |BF| ≤ 1 everywhere — which forces its height to stay O(log n) . Multiple choice — what makes a tree strictly balanced? (your quiz) Multiple choice A tree is strictly balanced if all of its nodes have… 0 or 2 children a complete shape |BF| ≤ 1 log n height |BF| ≤ 1 at every node. The other options describe related-but-different ideas: "0 or 2 children" is a full tree; "complete shape" and "log n height" are consequences of balance, not the definition of it. Multiple choice A node's left subtree has height 2 and its right subtree has height 0. What is its balance factor, and is it allowed in an AVL tree? BF = 0, allowed BF = 2, NOT allowed (|BF| > 1) BF = −2, allowed BF = H(L) − H(R) = 2 − 0 = 2 . Since |2| > 1 , this node violates the AVL invariant → it must be rebalanced. Tip: compute BFs starting from the leaves (leaves have height 0, empty = height −1). T / F Perfect and complete binary trees are strictly balanced and have log n height. True False True (slide 6). They're the "most balanced" shapes — every node has |BF| ≤ 1 — which is exactly why their height is O(log n).

The path z → y → x (each step Left or Right) names the case: LL, RR, LR, RL . Order the steps to fix an imbalance (your quiz) Use ▲ / ▼ to arrange, then check. Stop at the first node with |BF| > 1 , rebalance it (find z/y/x, determine the case, rotate), and continue up. Each fix is O(1); the walk is O(log n). Which case? insert(4, 16, 8) into an empty AVL tree (your quiz) Multiple choice Starting empty, insert 4, then 16, then 8. What rebalancing case results? LL RR LR RL None, the tree is balanced RL . 4 is the root; 16 > 4 → right child; 8 < 16 → left child of 16. Now z = 4 (BF = −2), y = 16 (z's right child), x = 8 (y's left child). Path z→y→x = Right, then Left → RL → fix with a right rotation then a left rotation. Same-height tie-breaker Multiple choice If both children of y have the same height (either single or double rotation would balance it), which do the slides say to prefer? The single rotation (prefer LL over LR, and RR over RL) — it's faster The double rotation, always It doesn't matter and there's no preference Slide 17: prefer the single rotation (treat it as LL/RR rather than LR/RL) because one rotation is fewer operations than two. Both produce a valid AVL tree.

title: Lesson 13 · Time Complexity
text: Lesson 13 · Time Complexity Because an AVL tree stays balanced, its height is always O(log n) . Every operation is bounded by that height. Multiple choice — AVL operations (your quiz) Multiple choice The height, search, insertion, and deletion of an AVL tree are all… O(1) O(log n) O(n) O(n log n) O(n²) O(log n) . Height is O(log n) (balanced); search/insert/delete follow a root-to-leaf path = O(log n); walking back up to check balance = O(log n); and each rotation fix is O(1) . The guaranteed balance is what a plain BST lacks — a plain BST can degrade to O(n). Multiple choice Why is an AVL tree better than a plain BST for search-heavy workloads? A plain BST can degenerate to a "stick" (O(n)); the AVL tree guarantees O(log n) by rebalancing. AVL trees use less memory. AVL trees don't need comparisons. Recall from L11: a plain BST's shape depends on insert order and can become a linked list (O(n)). title: Lesson 13 · Code Writing — A8 recursive style
text: Lesson 13 · Code Writing — A8 recursive style This matches the A8 AVL assignment : there is no separate Node class — each AVLTree<T> object is a subtree, with fields _value , _left , _right (both AVLTree<T> ), _height , _size . An empty tree is a real object ( _value=null , _height=-1 , _size=0 ), and a non-empty node's children are empty AVLTree objects, never null . Rotations/fixes are methods on this that return the new subtree root . The rule that trips everyone up: recapture the result Multiple choice Why write _left = (AVLTree<T>) _left.insert(element); instead of just _left.insert(element); ? To make it compile. A rotation inside the child can change which object is the child's root, so you must reassign _left to the returned root — otherwise the rebalanced subtree is lost. Because insert is static. Self-balancing means insert / remove can return a different root object. Throw away the return value and any rotation below is lost. Always recapture the result into the child field. (This is why the interface methods return the tree.) T / F Because empty children are real AVLTree objects (not null ), you can call _left.height() without a null check. True False True — the empty-tree sentinel returns height −1 and size 0, so the recursive calls just work. That's the payoff of using empty objects instead of null children. 1. updateHeightAndSize & balanceFactor Recompute this node's stats from its children (empty child → height −1, size 0). Balance factor = left height − right height. Show solution private void updateHeightAndSize () { _height = 1 + Math.max(_left.height(), _right.height()); _size = 1 + _left.size() + _right.size(); } private int balanceFactor () { return _left.height() - _right.height(); // H(L) - H(R) } No null checks needed. Call updateHeightAndSize() after any structural change — after a rotation, and after an insert/remove recursion returns. 2. rotateRight & rotateLeft (called on this ) No parameter — they rotate this down and return the new root. Update heights on this first (it dropped), then on the new root. rotateRight() { ... }"> Show solution private AVLTree<T> rotateRight () { AVLTree<T> newRoot = _left; _left = newRoot._right; // hand off newRoot's right subtree newRoot._right = this ; // this drops to newRoot's right this .updateHeightAndSize(); // this is now lower — update it first newRoot.updateHeightAndSize(); return newRoot; } private AVLTree<T> rotateLeft () { // mirror image AVLTree<T> newRoot = _right; _right = newRoot._left; newRoot._left = this ; this .updateHeightAndSize(); newRoot.updateHeightAndSize(); return newRoot; } Same three pointer moves as the generic rotation, just as instance methods on the node being rotated down. rotateLeft is rotateRight with every left/right swapped. 3. fixIfImbalanced (the LL/RR/LR/RL dispatch) Update stats, read the balance factor, and if |BF| > 1 pick the case and rotate. Return the (possibly new) root. fixIfImbalanced() { ... }"> Show solution private AVLTree<T> fixIfImbalanced () { updateHeightAndSize(); int bf = balanceFactor(); if (bf > 1 ) { // left-heavy if (_left.balanceFactor() < 0 ) // LR: straighten child first _left = _left.rotateLeft(); return rotateRight(); // LL (or finish LR) } else if (bf < - 1 ) { // right-heavy if (_right.balanceFactor() > 0 ) // RL: straighten child first _right = _right.rotateRight(); return rotateLeft(); // RR (or finish RL) } return this ; // already balanced } Order matters: updateHeightAndSize() comes before reading balanceFactor() , or the BF is stale. The LR/RL child rotations use recapture ( _left = _left.rotateLeft() ) — same rule as insert. 4. insert Empty tree → become a one-node tree (with empty children). Otherwise BST-recurse with recapture , then fixIfImbalanced() . insert(T element) { ... }"> Show solution public SelfBalancingBST<T> insert (T element) { if (isEmpty()) { // fill this empty node _value = element; _left = new AVLTree<>(); _right = new AVLTree<>(); _height = 0 ; _size = 1 ; return this ; } int cmp = element.compareTo(_value); if (cmp < 0 ) _left = (AVLTree<T>) _left.insert(element); else if (cmp > 0 ) _right = (AVLTree<T>) _right.insert(element); else return this ; // duplicate — no change return fixIfImbalanced(); } A new value always lands in an empty AVLTree (height −1), which becomes a leaf with two empty children. Each recursion recaptures the child; the final fixIfImbalanced() rebalances on the way back up. 5. remove (the three delete cases) BST-remove, then rebalance. When you find the node: leaf → become empty; one child → return the other; two children → copy the successor (min of the right subtree) and remove it from the right. remove(T element) { ... }"> Show solution public SelfBalancingBST<T> remove (T element) { if (isEmpty()) return this ; // not found int cmp = element.compareTo(_value); if (cmp < 0 ) _left = (AVLTree<T>) _left.remove(element); else if (cmp > 0 ) _right = (AVLTree<T>) _right.remove(element); else { // found it if (_left.isEmpty() && _right.isEmpty()) { _value = null ; _left = null ; _right = null ; _height = - 1 ; _size = 0 ; return this ; // leaf → become empty } else if (_left.isEmpty()) return _right; // one child else if (_right.isEmpty()) return _left; else { // two children T successor = _right.findMin(); _value = successor; _right = (AVLTree<T>) _right.remove(successor); } } return fixIfImbalanced(); } Two-children case: copy the successor (smallest value in the right subtree) into this node, then remove that successor from the right — it's guaranteed to be an easy leaf/one-child delete. Every branch ends by rebalancing with fixIfImbalanced() .

title: Lesson 14 · Red-Black Tree Invariants
text: Lesson 14 · Red-Black Tree Invariants A Red-Black tree is another self-balancing BST . It's a normal BST plus five color rules that together keep the height O(log n) — but with a looser balance than AVL, so it needs fewer rotations on insert/delete. The five properties Color — choose — Every node is either red or black The root is black Leaves (the NIL null pointers) are black A red node cannot have red children (no two reds in a row) Every path from a node down to its NIL leaves passes through the same number of black nodes Root — choose — Every node is either red or black The root is black Leaves (the NIL null pointers) are black A red node cannot have red children (no two reds in a row) Every path from a node down to its NIL leaves passes through the same number of black nodes Leaves — choose — Every node is either red or black The root is black Leaves (the NIL null pointers) are black A red node cannot have red children (no two reds in a row) Every path from a node down to its NIL leaves passes through the same number of black nodes Red — choose — Every node is either red or black The root is black Leaves (the NIL null pointers) are black A red node cannot have red children (no two reds in a row) Every path from a node down to its NIL leaves passes through the same number of black nodes Black — choose — Every node is either red or black The root is black Leaves (the NIL null pointers) are black A red node cannot have red children (no two reds in a row) Every path from a node down to its NIL leaves passes through the same number of black nodes Check The "same number of black nodes on every path" count is called the black height . Why it stays balanced Multiple choice What do the color rules guarantee about the tree's shape? Every node has exactly two children. The longest root-to-leaf path is at most twice the shortest, so the height is at most 2·log₂(n+1) = O(log n). The tree is always perfectly balanced like an AVL tree. The "no two reds in a row" + "equal black height" rules force the longest path to be ≤ 2× the shortest → height O(log n). It's a looser balance than AVL (which is ~1.44·log n), which is the trade-off. T / F If the insertion process ever leaves the root red, you can simply recolor the root black without breaking anything. True False True (slide 4). Recoloring the root from red to black adds one black node to every root-to-leaf path equally, so the black-height property still holds.

title: Lesson 14 · Insertion
text: Lesson 14 · Insertion Insert like a normal BST, color the new node red (root → black), then fix any red-red violation. The fix depends on the pibling (the parent's sibling — the new node's "aunt/uncle"): red pibling → recolor ; black pibling → rotate . Order the insertion steps Use ▲ / ▼ to arrange, then check. Check order Recolor or rotate? Multiple choice You insert a red node, its parent is red, and the pibling is also red . What do you do? Recolor: set parent and pibling to black, grandparent to red, then re-check from the grandparent (traverse up). Rotate immediately. Delete the new node. Red pibling → recolor (push the "blackness" down from the grandparent). Because the grandparent turned red, you must re-check upward — the violation may have moved up the tree. Multiple choice Parent is red but the pibling is black (or NIL). What do you do? Recolor parent and pibling. Rotate: figure out the LL / RR / LR / RL path from grandparent to the new node, rotate accordingly, set the new subtree root black and its children red. Nothing — it's already valid. Black pibling → rotate (same LL/RR/LR/RL cases as AVL!), then recolor: new subtree root black, its two children red. After a rotation fix you're done — no need to keep traversing up.

title: Lesson 14 · Deletion (the double-black idea)
text: Lesson 14 · Deletion (the double-black idea) Delete like a normal BST. The tricky case is removing a black leaf — that removes a black node from one path, breaking the black-height rule. Mark the NIL that replaced it as a "double black" and resolve it back to a single black through recoloring/rotation cases. Color arithmetic Think of colors as levels of "blackness," weakest → strongest: R < B < DB (double black). Combining rules: R + DB = B R + B = B B + B = DB Multiple choice Why does deleting a black leaf create a problem, but deleting a red leaf doesn't? Red leaves can't be deleted. Removing a black node drops the black count on that path by one, breaking the equal-black-height rule; a red node isn't counted in black height, so removing it changes nothing. Black leaves are always the root. Black height only counts black nodes. Delete a red leaf → no black-count change → fine. Delete a black leaf → that path is now short one black → the "double black" placeholder tracks the deficit until you fix it. Multiple choice When resolving a double black, the sibling is black with two black children . What happens? Rotate immediately. Delete the sibling. Recolor the sibling red and push the double-black up to the parent (if the parent was black, keep going up; if red, it absorbs the extra black and you stop). Sibling black + 2 black children → recolor sibling red, move the "extra black" up to the parent. This is the case that can propagate up the tree , like the recolor case in insertion. (Sibling red, or sibling with a red child, are handled by rotations instead.) Animated walkthrough — delete(J, G, Z) Step through each deletion on the sample tree. title: Lesson 14 · Code Writing
text: Lesson 14 · Code Writing A red-black node is a BST node plus a color. A common convention: null children count as black , which makes the color checks clean. 1. The node + an isRed helper Write an enum Color , a node with a _color field, and isRed(node) (null = black). Show solution enum Color { RED, BLACK } class RBNode { int _value; Color _color; RBNode _left, _right; } private boolean isRed (RBNode n) { return n != null && n._color == Color.RED; // null (NIL) is black } Treating null as black matches the "Leaves are black" invariant and means you never have to null-check a color separately. 2. The recolor step (red-pibling case) Given a node whose parent and pibling are both red, write the recolor: parent & pibling → black, grandparent → red. Show solution private void recolor (RBNode parent, RBNode pibling, RBNode grandparent) { parent._color = Color.BLACK; pibling._color = Color.BLACK; grandparent._color = Color.RED; // grandparent is now red, so re-check the violation from grandparent upward } This "pushes blackness down" from the grandparent to its two children. Because the grandparent became red, you loop again treating it as the newly-inserted node — the fix may cascade up to the root (which you then just recolor black). 3. Rotations (reused from AVL) The black-pibling fix uses the same rotateLeft / rotateRight as AVL — the LL/RR/LR/RL cases are identical. Write rotateRight . Show solution private RBNode rotateRight (RBNode z) { RBNode y = z._left; z._left = y._right; // hand off y's right subtree y._right = z; return y; // y is the new subtree root } Structurally identical to the AVL rotation (Lesson 13) — the only new work in a red-black tree is the recoloring around it: after the rotation, set the new subtree root black and its children red.

title: Lesson 15 · Comparing Self-Balancing Trees
text: Lesson 15 · Comparing Self-Balancing Trees AVL and red-black trees both guarantee O(log n), but they trade off differently. AVL keeps a tighter balance (|BF| ≤ 1) → shorter trees → faster search , but more rotations per update. Red-black allows a looser balance (longest path ≤ 2× shortest) → fewer rotations → faster insert/delete . Match each tree to its edge Plain BST — choose — No self-balancing — can degrade to O(n) if inserts are unlucky Tightest balance → best for search-heavy workloads Looser balance, fewer rotations → best for insert/delete-heavy workloads AVL Tree — choose — No self-balancing — can degrade to O(n) if inserts are unlucky Tightest balance → best for search-heavy workloads Looser balance, fewer rotations → best for insert/delete-heavy workloads Red-Black Tree — choose — No self-balancing — can degrade to O(n) if inserts are unlucky Tightest balance → best for search-heavy workloads Looser balance, fewer rotations → best for insert/delete-heavy workloads Check Multiple choice Why do standard libraries usually pick red-black over AVL? Red-black trees are always shorter. Red-black trees rebalance with fewer rotations, so inserts/deletes are faster — and most workloads mix reads and writes. AVL trees can't do deletion. Both are O(log n), but AVL's stricter balance means more rotations per update. Red-black's looser balance keeps updates cheap while lookups stay O(log n) — a good all-round default.

title: Lesson 16 · Hash Functions & Load
text: Lesson 16 · Hash Functions & Load A hash function maps a key to an index in 0..M-1 (M = table size), usually with modular arithmetic ( mod M ) so any integer "loops around" into the table. Example: h("Bob") = (66+111+98) mod 10 = 275 mod 10 = 5 . A good hash function runs in O(1) and distributes keys uniformly . Load factor Load factor = N / M — the number of stored elements over the table size. It drives the collision probability: N << M → few collisions; N ≈ M → many collisions (and probing breaks down). Multiple choice A table of size M = 20 holds N = 5 keys. What is the load factor? 4.0 0.25 15 0.25 (= 5/20). Low load → collisions are rare → operations stay near O(1). Multiple choice Which hash function for strings gives a more uniform distribution (M = 26)? h(s) = (sum of ASCII codes) mod 26 h(s) = index of the first letter They're identical. Summing all characters mixes far more information than just the first letter, so keys spread out more evenly. "First letter" clumps everything under common starting letters (lots of names start with 'a'/'s'). Why a prime table size? T / F Making the table size M a prime number helps, because it avoids M sharing a common divisor with the keys (which would waste slots). True False True (slide 48). If keys are multiples of 4 and M = 12, they only ever land on multiples of 4 → clustering. A prime M has no common divisor with the keys, spreading them out.

title: Lesson 16 · Probing & Clustering
text: Lesson 16 · Probing & Clustering Open addressing / probing stores everything in the array itself — on a collision, it probes for the next open slot. Linear: h(k,i) = (k + i) mod M . Quadratic: h(k,i) = (k + i²) mod M . Here i is the collision number (0, 1, 2, …). Primary vs. secondary clustering Primary clustering (linear probing) — choose — Long runs of filled slots merge into big blocks; any key hashing near a block extends it Keys with the SAME initial hash follow the SAME probe path, clumping along it Secondary clustering (quadratic probing) — choose — Long runs of filled slots merge into big blocks; any key hashing near a block extends it Keys with the SAME initial hash follow the SAME probe path, clumping along it Check Quadratic probing avoids primary clustering but still has secondary clustering — and can even fail to insert (it may cycle through a limited set of slots). The quadratic-probing trap (your quiz) M = 8, h(k, i) = (k + i²) mod 8 . Insert 5, 22, 9, then 13. What index is 13 inserted at? Multiple choice Where does 13 go? 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 Cannot be inserted Cannot be inserted. First: 5→5, 22→6, 9→1. Now 13's probes: i²mod8 cycles through {0,1,4,1,0,1,4,1}, so (13 + that) mod 8 only ever gives indices 5, 6, 1 — all occupied! It never reaches the empty slots (0,2,3,4,7). That's secondary clustering causing an insertion failure. The deletion problem (linear probing) Multiple choice Why can't you just blank out a slot when deleting from a probing table? Deletion is impossible in a hash table. It would make the table bigger. An empty slot signals "not present" to searches, so blanking a slot could cut off the probe path to a later key. Use a tombstone flag instead. Search stops at the first truly-empty slot. If you blank a deleted slot in the middle of a cluster, a later key that probed past it becomes unreachable. Mark deletions with a tombstone (flag) that search skips over but insert can reuse. T / F When the probability of collision is high, chaining is generally better than linear probing. (your quiz) True False True. As N approaches M, linear probing suffers heavy clustering and breaks down, while chaining still works (chains just get a bit longer). Chaining degrades more gracefully at high load.

title: Lesson 16 · Double Hashing
text: Lesson 16 · Double Hashing Double hashing uses a second hash function to decide the probe step size, so keys that share an initial index still follow different probe paths: h(k, i) = (h1(k) + i · h2(k)) mod M . This avoids both primary and secondary clustering. The three probe steps Linear probing — choose — Step + 1 each time: (k + i) mod M Step + i² each time: (k + i²) mod M Step + h2(k) each time: (h1(k) + i·h2(k)) mod M Quadratic probing — choose — Step + 1 each time: (k + i) mod M Step + i² each time: (k + i²) mod M Step + h2(k) each time: (h1(k) + i·h2(k)) mod M Double hashing — choose — Step + 1 each time: (k + i) mod M Step + i² each time: (k + i²) mod M Step + h2(k) each time: (h1(k) + i·h2(k)) mod M Check Which are collision-resolution techniques? title: Lesson 16 · Code Writing
text: Lesson 16 · Code Writing A hash function turns a key into an index; the collision strategy decides where to actually store it. 1. A string hash function Write hash(String s, int M) = (sum of the characters' codes) mod M. Show solution int hash (String s, int M) { int sum = 0 ; for ( int i = 0 ; i < s.length(); i++) sum += s.charAt(i); // char auto-promotes to its int code return sum % M; // map into 0..M-1 } O(1) if string lengths are bounded. The final mod M is what constrains the result to a valid table index. 2. put with linear probing Write put(int key) for an int[] table of size M using linear probing (empty slots hold -1 ). Assume there is room. Show solution void put ( int key) { int i = 0 ; int idx = key % M; while (table[idx] != - 1 ) { // occupied → probe next i++; idx = (key + i) % M; // linear: step by 1 } table[idx] = key; } Swap the one line (key + i) % M for (key + i*i) % M to get quadratic probing, or (key%M + i*h2(key)) % M for double hashing. For deletion, use a tombstone value the search skips but put can overwrite.

title: Lesson 17 · Load Factor
text: Lesson 17 · Load Factor The load factor measures how full the table is: load = N / M (number of elements ÷ table size). It's the main driver of collision probability — the fuller the table, the more collisions. Example: N = 60, M = 100 → load = 0.6 . Fill in — the load factor formula (your quiz) Load factor is / . Check both Answer: N (# of elements in table) / M (table size). Higher load → higher collision probability. Multiple choice A table of size M = 40 holds N = 30 elements. What is the load? 1.33 0.75 10 0.75 (= 30/40). For probing this has hit the recommended resize threshold — time to grow the table.

title: Lesson 17 · Table Resizing
text: Lesson 17 · Table Resizing When the load gets too high (or too low), resize the table: allocate a new, larger (or smaller) array and reinsert every element . Because M changed, every hash value must be recomputed — you can't just copy the slots over. This is a lot like ArrayList doubling , but with re-hashing. Recommended thresholds Resize when N/M > T for a threshold T . Chaining tolerates a fuller table than probing, so it gets a higher threshold: • Chaining: T c = 1.0 (100%) — chains still work past load 1. • Probing: T p = 0.75 (75%) — clustering makes probing break down before the table is full. Multiple choice What does T p = 0.75 mean? (your quiz) Load of the hash table is 0.75 Average number of probes per operation is 0.75 Probability of collision is 0.75 when probing Resize if load > 0.75 when probing Resize if load > 0.75 when probing. T p is the threshold that triggers a resize — when the probing table passes 75% full, double it and reinsert. Multiple choice Why must resizing recompute every hash value? The keys change during resizing. The hash function uses mod M , and M just changed — so old indices are no longer valid. It doesn't; you can copy slots directly. Since h(k) = … mod M , changing M changes where every key belongs. You reinsert each element through the hash function against the new M. T / F Tables also need to be resized smaller if the load becomes too low. True False True (slide 5). A mostly-empty table wastes memory, so resizing shrinks it when load drops too far — just like ArrayList can shrink.

title: Lesson 17 · Time Complexity
text: Lesson 17 · Time Complexity The key distinction is worst case vs amortized . Worst case assumes everything collided into one slot/cluster. Amortized averages the occasional expensive resize (O(n) to reinsert all) across the many cheap operations, and — with a good hash function keeping the load bounded — comes out to O(1) . With resizing Worst case Amortized Insert / Search / Delete O(n) O(1) Multiple choice With resizing, all operations (insert, search, delete) have what worst-case time? (your quiz) O(1) O(log n) O(n) O(n²) O(n) . In the worst case every key collided into one chain/cluster (and a resize reinserts all n elements), so a single operation can touch all n. Multiple choice With resizing, all operations have what amortized time? (your quiz) O(1) O(log n) O(n) O(n²) O(1) . Resizing keeps the load bounded, so the average chain length / probe count stays constant. The rare O(n) resize is spread across many O(1) operations — exactly like ArrayList's amortized O(1) add. Multiple choice With a good hash function and resizing, the amortized average number of elements per chain is… N N/M, which stays bounded (≈ constant) because resizing caps the load → O(1) search M/N, which grows without bound A uniform hash spreads N keys over M slots → N/M per chain on average. Resizing keeps N/M under the threshold, so it's effectively constant → O(1) amortized search.

title: Lesson 17 · Code Writing
text: Lesson 17 · Code Writing Resizing is the mechanism that keeps a hash table's amortized operations O(1). 1. Decide when to resize Write needsResize() for a probing table (threshold 0.75) with fields int n and int m . Show solution boolean needsResize () { return ( double ) n / m > 0.75 ; // load past Tp → grow } Cast to double so you don't do integer division. For chaining, use 1.0 instead of 0.75 . 2. Resize & rehash Write resize() that doubles the table and reinserts every key (chaining table = array of linked lists). Assume a working put(key) that hashes against the current m . Show solution void resize () { List<Integer>[] old = table; // keep a handle on old contents m = m * 2 ; // grow (a prime near 2m is even better) table = new List[m]; // fresh, empty, larger table n = 0 ; // put() will re-count for (List<Integer> chain : old) if (chain != null ) for ( int key : chain) put(key); // re-hash against the NEW m } The whole operation is O(n) — but it only happens after ~n cheap inserts, so it amortizes to O(1) per insert (same argument as ArrayList doubling). The crucial line is re-running put so each key is hashed against the new M.

title: Lesson 18 · Sorting Recap (Heap Sort & Quick Sort)

Heap sort = BuildHeap (make a max-heap, O(n)) then repeatedly swap the root to the end and bubble down (O(n log n)) — all in place , O(1) space. Quick sort is O(n log n) average but O(n²) worst (presorted input, bad pivots). Sort comparison Sort Time (avg) Time (worst) Space Quick sort O(n log n) O(n²) O(log n) stack Heap sort O(n log n) O(n log n) O(1) in place Multiple choice What triggers quick sort's O(n²) worst case? A random pivot. A presorted (or nearly presorted) array, so each partition is maximally unbalanced. An array of all equal elements only. Presorted input with a naive pivot makes every partition split into sizes 0 and n−1 → n levels of O(n) work → O(n²). (Slides 6–7.) Heap sort avoids this — it's O(n log n) even in the worst case.

title: Lesson 19 · Topological Sort
text: Lesson 19 · Topological Sort A topological sort orders the vertices of a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) so that for every edge (u, v) , u comes before v . Think course prerequisites: you must take the prereq before the course. Every DAG has at least one topo order; some have many. A graph with a cycle has none — no vertex in the cycle can legally come first. In-degree & out-degree In-degree = number of edges pointing into a vertex. Out-degree = number of edges pointing out . Key cycle check (slide 3): if no vertex has in-degree 0, the graph must contain a cycle — because a topo sort has to start somewhere with nothing before it. T / F If a graph has at least one vertex with no in-edge and at least one vertex with no out-edge, it has a topo sort. (your quiz) True False False. A source (in-degree 0) and a sink (out-degree 0) do not rule out a cycle elsewhere in the graph. Topo sort exists only for DAGs — the graph must be completely acyclic . The in-degree-0 rule is necessary (no such vertex ⇒ cycle) but not sufficient . (Slide 3.) Multiple choice Why is a topo sort impossible when the graph has a cycle? Cycles make the graph undirected. Every vertex in the cycle depends on another in the cycle, so none can come first. Cycles remove all edges. In a cycle A→B→C→A, A must precede B, B precede C, and C precede A — a contradiction. No valid "first" vertex exists. (Slide 3.)

title: Lesson 19 · Topo Sort Algorithm (Kahn's)
text: Lesson 19 · Topo Sort Algorithm (Kahn's) Repeatedly pull off vertices that have nothing left before them: 1. Compute every vertex's in-degree; put all in-degree-0 vertices in a queue. 2. Dequeue a vertex v , append it to the output list. 3. "Remove" v : for each edge v→w , decrement w's in-degree. If w hits 0 , enqueue it. 4. Repeat until the queue is empty. If the output has fewer than |V| vertices → a cycle exists. So every order looks like 1 · (2,3 in either order) · 4 · (5,6 in either order) = 2 × 2 = 4 . E.g. 1,2,3,4,5,6 and 1,3,2,4,6,5. Animated walkthrough — Kahn's algorithm step-by-step Same graph. title: Lesson 19 · Breadth-First Search
text: Lesson 19 · Breadth-First Search BFS finds the shortest path (fewest hops) from a source s to every other vertex in an unweighted graph. It explores level by level using a FIFO queue — exactly like a tree's level-order traversal, but graphs can have cycles, so you must track which vertices you've already visited . The algorithm (slides 24–26) // d(v)=distance, p(v)=predecessor for each v: d(v) = ∞ d(s) = 0 ; mark s visited; enqueue s while Q not empty: u = dequeue() for each unvisited neighbor v of u: mark v visited d(v) = d(u) + 1 p(v) = u enqueue v What BFS tracks per vertex (your quiz) When running BFS, we track for each vertex whether it is , its from the source, and its along the path. Check all Answers: visited , distance (d(v)), predecessor (p(v)). Slides 23–24 list exactly these three: "Visited?", "d(v) = distance estimate from source", "p(v) = predecessor of v along the path". Distance gives shortest hop-count; predecessors let you reconstruct the actual path. Multiple choice Why does BFS need a "visited" flag but a tree's level-order traversal doesn't? Graphs are always weighted. A graph can have cycles, so without marking visited you'd revisit vertices forever. Trees don't use a queue. A tree has no cycles, so you never reach the same node twice. A graph "is not a tree anymore ⇒ may be cyclic" (slide 22), so the visited set stops infinite revisiting and keeps each vertex's first (shortest) distance. Insertion order (slides 29–30) If you enqueue a vertex's neighbors in a different order (e.g. reverse-alphabetical instead of alphabetical), the shortest-path tree can change — a vertex reachable from two vertices at the same level may get a different predecessor. But the distances d(v) stay the same , because the shortest hop-count doesn't depend on tie-breaking. Multiple choice You rerun BFS enqueuing neighbors in reverse order. What changes? Both the tree and the distances change. Neither changes. The shortest-path tree may change, but the distances stay the same. Slide 30: tree = NO (not the same), distances = YES (same). Tie-breaking on enqueue order only affects which equal-length path you record (the predecessor), never the length itself.

title: Lesson 19 · Code Writing
text: Lesson 19 · Code Writing 1. BFS shortest distances Given an adjacency list Map<V, List<V>> adj and a source s , return a map of shortest hop-distances. bfs(Map > adj, V s) { ... }"> Show solution Map <V,Integer> bfs ( Map <V,List<V>> adj, V s) { Map <V,Integer> dist = new HashMap<>(); Queue <V> q = new LinkedList<>(); dist.put(s, 0 ); // source distance 0 = "visited" q.add(s); while (!q.isEmpty()) { V u = q.remove(); // FIFO dequeue for (V v : adj.get(u)) { if (!dist.containsKey(v)) { // unvisited dist.put(v, dist.get(u) + 1 ); q.add(v); } } } return dist; } Using the dist map itself as the visited-set (a key exists ⇔ visited) is a common trick. Add a parallel Map<V,V> pred and set pred.put(v,u) to also recover the path. O(|V|+|E|). 2. Topological sort (Kahn's algorithm) Return a topo order, or an empty list if a cycle exists. topoSort(Map > adj) { ... }"> Show solution List <V> topoSort ( Map <V,List<V>> adj) { Map <V,Integer> indeg = new HashMap<>(); for (V v : adj.keySet()) indeg.putIfAbsent(v, 0 ); for (V u : adj.keySet()) // count in-degrees for (V v : adj.get(u)) indeg.merge(v, 1 , Integer::sum); Queue <V> q = new LinkedList<>(); for (V v : indeg.keySet()) // all in-degree-0 vertices if (indeg.get(v) == 0 ) q.add(v); List <V> order = new ArrayList<>(); while (!q.isEmpty()) { V u = q.remove(); order.add(u); for (V v : adj.get(u)) { // "remove" edge u->v indeg.merge(v, - 1 , Integer::sum); if (indeg.get(v) == 0 ) q.add(v); } } return order.size() == indeg.size() ? order : new ArrayList<>(); // cycle? } Decrementing in-degree as you "remove" each source is the whole trick — a vertex becomes enqueue-able exactly when its last incoming edge is removed. If the final list is short of |V|, some vertices were stuck in a cycle. O(|V|+|E|).

title: Lesson 20 · Dijkstra's Algorithm
text: Lesson 20 · Dijkstra's Algorithm Dijkstra solves single-source shortest path on graphs with non-negative weights. It's a greedy algorithm: always finalize the closest unvisited vertex next, using a min-heap priority queue keyed on the distance estimate d(v) . A vertex is marked visited only once its shortest path is settled . The algorithm (slide 8) Dijkstra(G, s): for each v: d(v) = ∞; d(s) = 0 add all vertices to a min-heap PQ keyed on d(v) while PQ not empty: u = dequeueMin() // closest unvisited vertex mark u visited for each unvisited neighbor v of u: Relax(u, v) // update d(v), p(v) if shorter Multiple choice Why does Dijkstra use a min -heap keyed on d(v)? To store the graph edges. To always pull out the closest unvisited vertex next — the greedy choice that turns out to be globally optimal. Because BFS uses one. Greedy: the unvisited vertex with the smallest estimate already has its final shortest distance (with non-negative weights), so we finalize it and relax its neighbors. The min-heap makes "find closest" efficient. (Slides 6–8.) Time complexity (slide 19) With the practical "enqueue a new entry instead of updating" version: the PQ grows up to O(m), so each enqueue/dequeue is O(log m) = O(log n²) = O(log n) . Overall: O((n + m) log n) . Sparse → O(n log n); dense → O(n² log n). Multiple choice Dijkstra's overall time complexity (heap-based) is… O(n + m) O(nm) O((n + m) log n) O((n + m) log n). Each vertex/edge triggers heap operations costing O(log n). (Slide 19.) It's slower than BFS's O(n+m) — the price of handling weights.

title: Lesson 20 · Bellman-Ford
text: Lesson 20 · Bellman-Ford Dijkstra fails with negative-weight edges — its greedy "finalize the closest vertex" assumption breaks, because a later negative edge could still lower a distance it already locked in. Bellman-Ford handles negative weights by relaxing every edge , n − 1 times . The algorithm (slides 25–29) BellmanFord(G, s): for each v: d(v) = ∞; d(s) = 0 for i = 1 to n - 1 : // n-1 passes for each edge (u,v): Relax(u,v) for each edge (u,v): // one more pass = cycle check if d(u) + w(u,v) < d(v): return FALSE // negative cycle! return TRUE Why n − 1 passes? A shortest path visits at most n vertices, so it has at most n − 1 edges; each pass locks in one more edge of every shortest path. The final extra pass detects a negative cycle : if anything still improves, no shortest path exists. What does Bellman-Ford return? (your quiz) Directed graph, source P. Edges: P→Q(2), P→R(4), Q→S(2), R→S(4), R→T(3), T→S(−5). T / F Bellman-Ford returns TRUE for this graph from source P. True False True. The graph has a negative edge (−5) but no negative cycle (you can't loop back around to keep decreasing). Bellman-Ford returns FALSE only when a negative cycle exists; here it computes valid shortest paths and returns TRUE. Negative edges are fine — negative cycles are the problem. Multiple choice When does Bellman-Ford return FALSE? Whenever any edge weight is negative. Only when the graph contains a negative-weight cycle reachable from the source. When the graph is disconnected. FALSE means "no shortest path exists" — which happens only with a negative cycle , where you could loop forever driving distances toward −∞. A lone negative edge is fine. (Slide 26, step c.) Time complexity (slide 30) Multiple choice Bellman-Ford's time complexity is… O((n+m) log n) O(nm) O(n + m) O(nm). It does n − 1 passes, each relaxing all m edges → O(n·m). Sparse: O(n²); dense: O(n³). Slower than Dijkstra, but it's the price of handling negative weights. (Slide 30.)

text: Lesson 20 · Code Writing 1. Relax an edge Write relax(u, v, w) updating Map<V,Integer> d and Map<V,V> p . Show solution void relax (V u, V v, int w) { if (d.get(u) + w < d.get(v)) { d.put(v, d.get(u) + w); // shorter path found p.put(v, u); // record predecessor } } This one three-line operation is the heart of both Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford — they differ only in what order and how many times they relax edges. 2. Bellman-Ford Return false if a negative cycle exists, else true . Edges as int[]{u,v,w} in list edges ; n vertices. Show solution boolean bellmanFord (V s) { for (V v : vertices) d.put(v, INF); d.put(s, 0 ); for ( int i = 1 ; i < n; i++) // n-1 passes for (Edge e : edges) relax (e.u, e.v, e.w); for (Edge e : edges) // cycle-detection pass if (d.get(e.u) + e.w < d.get(e.v)) return false ; // still improving = negative cycle return true ; } n − 1 passes over all m edges → O(nm). The extra pass at the end: if any edge still relaxes after n−1 passes, a negative cycle exists and no shortest path is defined.

title: Lesson 21 · Kruskal's Algorithm
text: Lesson 21 · Kruskal's Algorithm Kruskal builds the MST by adding edges smallest weight first , skipping any edge that would form a cycle . It's a greedy algorithm — the locally cheapest safe edge each step gives the globally cheapest tree. It starts as a forest of single vertices and merges them into one tree. Very fast on sparse graphs. (Slides 8–9.) The steps (slide 9) 1. Start with all vertices, no edges (a forest). 2. Sort edges; repeatedly take the minimum-weight edge. 3. if it connects two different trees → add it (merge). else (both endpoints already connected) → reject (would make a cycle). 4. Repeat until all vertices are in one tree (n − 1 edges). Multiple choice Kruskal rejects an edge when… Its weight is too large. Both of its endpoints are already in the same tree (adding it would create a cycle). It connects two different trees. Reject only on a cycle — when both endpoints are already connected. The "same tree?" test is done efficiently with a union-find structure. (Slide 9.) Multiple choice Kruskal's time complexity is dominated by… Building the heap, O(n). The union-find, O(n²). Sorting the edges: O(m log m). Great for sparse graphs. O(m log m) — sorting the m edges is the bottleneck (the union-find operations are nearly O(1) each). Since m is small in a sparse graph, Kruskal shines there. (Slide 8: "very fast on sparse graphs.")

title: Lesson 21 · Prim's Algorithm
text: Lesson 21 · Prim's Algorithm Prim grows one tree outward from a starting vertex. At each step it adds the cheapest edge that leaves the tree — connecting a vertex already in the tree to one that isn't. Because the new vertex is always outside the tree, it can never create a cycle . Also greedy. Better than Kruskal on dense graphs. (Slides 13–14.) The steps (slide 14) 1. Start with an empty tree T; pick any start vertex, add it to T. 2. Add the min-weight edge (u, v) where u is in T but v is not , and add v to T. 3. Repeat until all vertices are included. Fill in — Prim's growth rule (your quiz) In Prim's algorithm, each step adds to the tree the weight edge (u, v) where is in the tree but is not. Check all Answers: minimum weight edge (u, v) where u is in the tree but v is not. Since v is always outside T, this edge never forms a cycle. (Slide 14.) T / F Prim's algorithm is better than Kruskal's algorithm on dense graphs. (your quiz) True False True (slide 14). Prim grows one tree and doesn't need to sort all m edges, so on a dense graph (m ≈ n²) it beats Kruskal's O(m log m) sort. Kruskal wins on sparse graphs.

text: Lesson 21 · Code Writing 1. Kruskal's (with union-find) Return the total MST weight. Edges as int[]{u,v,w} ; n vertices numbered 0..n−1. edges, int n) { ... }"> Show solution int [] parent; int find ( int x){ return parent[x]==x ? x : (parent[x]= find (parent[x])); } int kruskal (List<int[]> edges, int n){ parent = new int [n]; for ( int i= 0 ; i<n; i++) parent[i]=i; // each vertex its own tree edges.sort((a,b) -> a[ 2 ] - b[ 2 ]); // smallest weight first int cost= 0 ; for ( int [] e : edges){ int ru= find (e[ 0 ]), rv= find (e[ 1 ]); if (ru != rv){ // different trees → no cycle parent[ru]=rv; // union cost += e[ 2 ]; } // else: same tree → skip (cycle) } return cost; } find with path compression makes the "same tree?" check nearly O(1). Sorting dominates → O(m log m). 2. Prim's (with a min-heap) Grow from vertex 0; adjacency list adj.get(u) gives int[]{v, w} pairs. > adj, int n) { ... }"> Show solution int prim ( Map <Integer,List<int[]>> adj, int n){ boolean [] inTree = new boolean [n]; PriorityQueue <int[]> pq = // {vertex, edgeWeight} new PriorityQueue<>((a,b) -> a[ 1 ] - b[ 1 ]); pq.add( new int []{ 0 , 0 }); // start vertex, cost 0 int cost= 0 ; while (!pq.isEmpty()){ int [] top = pq.poll(); int u = top[ 0 ]; if (inTree[u]) continue ; // already added → skip inTree[u] = true ; cost += top[ 1 ]; for ( int [] nb : adj.get(u)) // push leaving edges if (!inTree[nb[ 0 ]]) pq.add( new int []{nb[ 0 ], nb[ 1 ]}); } return cost; } The heap always hands back the cheapest edge leaving the current tree. Each edge is pushed once → O(m log n).

title: Lesson 6 · Encapsulation
text: Lesson 6 · Encapsulation Encapsulation — bundling data (fields) and methods into a single unit (a class) while restricting direct external access to that data. The recipe is two rules: (1) make all fields private , and (2) provide public methods — getters and/or setters — to retrieve or change them. Fill in — the encapsulation recipe For encapsulation, make all fields and provide getters and setters for those fields. Check both Straight from your quiz & slide 4: fields private (locked down), accessors public (the controlled doors in). Benefits — why bother? Multiple choice Which is NOT a benefit of encapsulation listed on the slides? You can make a "read-only" field by providing a getter but no setter. A setter can validate a new value to prevent illegal state. You can expose derived/complex properties computed from multiple fields. It makes your program run in less memory automatically. The three real benefits (slide 4): read-only fields (no setter), validating setters, and derived properties. Encapsulation is about control and safety , not automatic memory savings. Encapsulated vs. NOT — the danger In nonEncapsulated/ , Point 's fields have no private , so outside code can reach right in and corrupt a triangle: // Perimeter.java (nonEncapsulated) — this compiles and runs! t1._a._x += 5; // reaching directly into private data t1._a = t1._c; // now two corners are the same point Multiple choice Why is the encapsulated version (fields private ) safer? Outside code physically cannot touch the fields, so it can't put the object into a broken state — all changes must go through validated methods. Private fields make the math more accurate. Private fields run faster than public ones. With private fields, t1._a._x += 5 won't even compile. Callers are forced through methods that can enforce the object's rules (like the co-linearity check in the real Triangle ). T / F Interfaces achieve the same hiding idea as encapsulation: they expose public methods while letting each implementing class keep its internal fields and implementation hidden. True False True — slide 4 makes this link. An interface says what methods exist; the class hides how .

title: Lesson 6 · Interfaces
text: Lesson 6 · Interfaces A class defines a data type. An interface defines an abstract data type (ADT) — it lists a set of public methods that must be available, separating what a type can do from how it does it. It's a contract : any class that implements it promises to provide those methods. Anatomy of an interface Own file, like a class. Body is just method signatures — no bodies, no fields. From oneInterface/Point.java : public interface Point { double getX (); double getY (); double distanceTo (Point p); boolean equals (Point p); } T / F A normal interface method includes a body (the actual code) between curly braces. True False False — a method signature ends in a semicolon with no { } . The body lives in the implementing class. (Exception: default methods, below.) T / F An interface can define static methods/fields and default instance methods — but a default method may only call other interface methods, not access fields directly. True False Slide 9. A default method can provide a body because it relies only on other interface methods (e.g. get2X() calls getX() ) — it never touches fields, which interfaces don't have. // default method example (slide 9) public interface Point { double getX (); default double get2X () { return getX () * 2 ; // only uses another interface method } } Exposed vs. internal behavior Exposed behavior — choose — Public methods required by the interface(s) the class implements Hidden private helper methods used internally Internal behavior — choose — Public methods required by the interface(s) the class implements Hidden private helper methods used internally Check In PointTriangle , getArea() / getPerimeter() are exposed (in the Triangle interface), while sideABLength() and checkColinearity() are private — internal implementation detail.

title: Lesson 6 · Implementing an Interface & Interface Types
text: Lesson 6 · Implementing an Interface & Interface Types A class implements an interface with class X implements A, B and must declare every interface method as public . The interface name can then be used as a type — a variable of that type can hold any object whose class implements it. But you cannot instantiate an interface directly . The header public class CartesianPoint implements Point { // must define getX, getY, distanceTo, equals — all public } Fill in If Dog implements the Animal interface, declare an Animal variable named dog instantiated as a Dog (no constructor args): Check Answer: Animal dog = new Dog(); — the variable type is the interface ( Animal ), the object is a concrete class ( Dog ). text: Lesson 6 · Abstract Data Types (ADTs) An ADT is the idea of defining and reasoning about a data type by its behavior, not its implementation . A class that implements the interface is a concrete implementation , and one ADT may have many implementations (which can differ in performance/memory). title: Lesson 7 · Binary Search — O(log n)
text: Lesson 7 · Binary Search — O(log n) Binary search finds a key in a sorted array by repeatedly checking the middle element and throwing away half the array each time: if the middle equals the key, done; if the key is smaller, search the bottom half; if larger, search the top half. Halving each step gives O(log n) . Worked trace Search for key = 10 in the sorted array a = [3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 20, 25] (n = 7). Step 1: whole array, middle index 3 → a[3] = 6. 10 > 6 → search TOP half. Step 2: [10, 20, 25], middle → 20. 10 < 20 → search BOTTOM half. Step 3: [10], middle → 10. 10 == 10 → FOUND (3 steps). Multiple choice Why must the array be sorted for binary search to work? Sorting makes the array smaller. So the middle element is always the answer. Because comparing to the middle only tells you which half to keep if the data is in order. Sorted order is what lets one comparison eliminate half the elements. On unsorted data, "less than the middle" tells you nothing about where the key is. Fill in The time complexity of binary search is Check Answer: O(log n) . Each step halves the search space, so it takes about log₂ n + 1 steps. (This relies on a[i] being O(1) — true for arrays, but not for every data structure!) T / F Binary search is O(log n) no matter what data structure holds the data. True False False — it's O(log n) because array indexing a[i] is O(1). On a structure where reaching the middle isn't O(1) (e.g. a linked list), the analysis changes. Complexity depends on the data structure used.

title: Lesson 7 · Quick Sort — divide & conquer
text: Lesson 7 · Quick Sort — divide & conquer Quick sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm: pick a pivot , partition the array so everything smaller than the pivot is on its left and everything larger is on its right (the pivot lands in its final sorted spot), then recurse on the left and right sub-arrays. Base case: a sub-array of one element is already sorted. The steps Multiple choice After one partition around a pivot, what is guaranteed? The whole array is sorted. The pivot is in its final sorted position, with all smaller elements left of it and all larger right of it. The array is reversed. Partitioning fixes the pivot's final spot and splits the rest into "smaller" and "larger" groups. Those groups aren't sorted yet — that's what the recursive calls handle. T / F Quick sort's recursion bottoms out (base case) when a sub-array has only one element, since a single element is already sorted. True False True — a one-element sub-array needs no work, so the recursion stops there. Complexity — why two answers? Average case — choose — O(n log n) — pivots split the array roughly in half → ~log n levels, O(n) work per level O(n²) — a poor pivot barely splits the array → ~n levels, O(n) work per level Worst case — choose — O(n log n) — pivots split the array roughly in half → ~log n levels, O(n) work per level O(n²) — a poor pivot barely splits the array → ~n levels, O(n) work per level Check Both cases do O(n) work partitioning at each level. The difference is the number of levels : good pivots → ~log n levels (O(n log n)); bad pivots (already-sorted-ish input, always picking an extreme) → ~n levels (O(n²)). That's why the pivot is often chosen randomly.

title: Lesson 8 · Recursion vs. Iteration
text: Lesson 8 · Recursion vs. Iteration Many problems can be solved either recursively (a method calling itself) or iteratively (loops). Recursion is often more concise and closer to the problem's definition, but can have worse time complexity when it recomputes overlapping subproblems. Fill in — the trade-off (your quiz) For complex recursive problems, recursive approaches are often more and have a time complexity than iterative approaches. Check both Answers: concise and greater . Recursion reads cleaner, but the naive recursive version can blow up (see Fibonacci below). Fibonacci — two versions, same result Recursive — concise but O(2ⁿ) static int fib ( int x) { if (x == 0 ) return 0 ; if (x == 1 ) return 1 ; return fib (x- 1 ) + fib (x- 2 ); } Iterative — a bit longer but O(n) static int fib ( int x) { if (x == 0 ) return 0 ; if (x == 1 ) return 1 ; int [] f = new int [x]; f[ 1 ] = 1 ; for ( int i= 2 ; i<f.length; i++) f[i] = f[i- 1 ] + f[i- 2 ]; return f[x- 1 ]; } Multiple choice Why is the recursive Fibonacci O(2ⁿ) while the iterative one is O(n)? Recursion is always slower than loops. The iterative version skips the base cases. The recursive version recomputes the same fib(k) values over and over (overlapping subproblems); the iterative version computes each once and stores it. The recursion tree for fib branches twice per call and recomputes shared subtrees. The iterative version fills an array once, left to right — each value computed a single time. See it in the Diagram It tab. Dynamic Programming Dynamic Programming (DP) = solving a complex problem by breaking it into overlapping subproblems , solving each exactly once , and storing the results (e.g. in an array) to avoid redundant work. T / F A good strategy is to write the recursive solution first (since finding the base/recursive cases is the hard part), then convert it to an iterative one to cut the time complexity. True False True (slide 6). Think recursively to get it correct, then add storage / convert to iteration for speed — that's the DP mindset (the iterative Fibonacci above is exactly this).

title: Lesson 8 · Recursion Practice
text: Lesson 8 · Recursion Practice Recipe: break the problem into smaller subproblems, identify the base case(s) and recursive case(s) , then compute the time complexity (linear? divide-and-conquer? exponential?). Find the bug This divide-and-conquer sum (sum of data[start..end] ) has a bug. Trace it on a size-2 range and draw the recursion tree. static int sum ( int start, int end, int [] data) { if (start == end) return data[start]; int firstHalf = sum (start, (start+end)/ 2 , data); int secondHalf = sum ((start+end)/ 2 , end, data); // <-- ? return firstHalf + secondHalf; } Show the bug & fix Bug: the second call starts at the same index the first call ended on: mid = (start+end)/2 . So the middle element is counted in both halves, and worse — for a size-2 range (start, start+1) , mid = start , so the second call sum(start, start+1, ...) is identical to the original call → infinite recursion → StackOverflowError . Fix: start the second half one past the middle: int secondHalf = sum((start+end)/2 + 1, end, data); Time complexity of the fixed sum Multiple choice Once fixed, what's the time complexity in terms of n (the range size)? O(n) — each element is visited once at the leaves; the split tree has ~2n nodes doing O(1) work O(n²) O(2ⁿ) — like naive Fibonacci O(n) . It splits the range in half and recurses on non-overlapping halves ( T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(1) ), so every element is summed exactly once → linear. (Unlike Fibonacci, the subproblems here don't overlap.) String recursion — upgrade Write upgrade(String s) : replace every "110" with "210" (left to right, non-overlapping), leaving everything else unchanged. Show solution public static String upgrade (String s) { if (s.length() < 3 ) return s; // base: too short to match if (s.startsWith( "110" )) return "210" + upgrade (s.substring( 3 )); // match: consume 3 chars return s.charAt( 0 ) + upgrade (s.substring( 1 )); // no match: keep 1 char, recurse on rest } Two recursive cases: on a match, emit "210" and skip 3 chars; otherwise keep the first char and recurse on the rest. The substring is the shrinking argument that reaches the base case. String recursion — pairCount Write pairCount(String s) : count how many characters equal the character two positions after them (i.e. s[i] == s[i+2] ). Show solution public static int pairCount (String s) { if (s.length() < 3 ) return 0 ; // base: no i+2 to compare if (s.charAt( 0 ) == s.charAt( 2 )) return 1 + pairCount (s.substring( 1 )); // count it + recurse return pairCount (s.substring( 1 )); // just recurse } Linear recursion: check the front pair, add 1 if it matches, then slide forward by one character. Base case when fewer than 3 chars remain. Divide the search — sumToTarget Write sumToTarget(int[] nums, int index, int target) : return true if some subset of nums[index..] sums to target . (Classic "include it or skip it" recursion.) Show solution boolean sumToTarget ( int [] nums, int index, int target) { if (target == 0 ) return true ; // hit it exactly if (index == nums.length || target < 0 ) return false ; return sumToTarget (nums, index+ 1 , target) // SKIP nums[index] || sumToTarget (nums, index+ 1 , target - nums[index]); // INCLUDE it } Two recursive calls = try every subset: one branch skips the current number, the other includes it (subtracting it from the target). Exponential in the worst case, but a clean, correct way to explore all combinations.

title: Lesson 8 · Generics
text: Lesson 8 · Generics A generic type <T> is a placeholder for a type , written in angle brackets. The letter doesn't matter ( <E> , <K, V> , …). It lets one class/method/interface work for any type ; you fill in the real type when you use it: Box<String> , Box<Integer> . You can declare several at once: <K, V> . Select all — what can declare a generic type?
