To store a primitive, use its wrapper class ( int → Integer , double → Double , char → Character …). Autoboxing converts between them automatically. Integer x = 5 ; // autobox: int -> Integer int y = x; // auto-unbox: Integer -> int List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>(); // List<int> is illegal Multiple choice Why is List<int> illegal but List<Integer> fine? Because int is bigger than Integer. A generic type argument must be a reference type (an object); int is a primitive, so you use its wrapper Integer . Because lists can't hold numbers. Generics only work with objects, so primitives ride in as their wrapper classes — and autoboxing makes it feel seamless ( nums.add(5) boxes the 5 into an Integer ).

title: Lesson 9 · List (the ADT)
text: Lesson 9 · List (the ADT) A List is an ADT (Lesson 6 idea): an interface describing behavior, with no implementation. It holds ordered elements indexed 0 to n-1 . Two classes implement it differently: ArrayList (elements in an array) and LinkedList (elements in linked nodes). Fill in — the two implementations ArrayLists store elements in an while LinkedLists store each element in its own . Check both Answers: array and node (matches your quiz). Same List contract, two very different underlying structures. The List<T> interface From list/List.java — a set of method signatures, no bodies: public interface List <T> { int size (); boolean isEmpty (); void clear (); boolean contains (T element); int find (T element); void add (T element); void add ( int index, T element); // overloaded boolean remove (T element); T remove ( int index); // overloaded T get ( int index); T set ( int index, T element); } T / F Having both add(T element) and add(int index, T element) is an example of method overloading — same name, different parameter lists. True False True (slide 14). Overloaded methods share a name but are distinguished by the number/types of parameters. The compiler picks the right one based on the arguments you pass. Multiple choice What does the <T> in List<T> mean? The list can only hold objects of a class literally named T. A generic type placeholder — you fill in the real type when you use it, e.g. List<Integer> or List<String> . It means the list is sorted. T is a generic placeholder. List<String> s = new ArrayList<>(); makes a list of Strings; the same class works for any element type.

title: Lesson 9 · ArrayList — a dynamic array
text: Lesson 9 · ArrayList — a dynamic array A plain Java array has a fixed size . An ArrayList fixes that: it stores elements in an array with some initial capacity (e.g. 4), and when the array gets full it allocates a bigger array (e.g. ×1.5) and copies everything over. Accessing a[i] stays O(1) . Using an ArrayList List<String> songs = new ArrayList <>(); songs.add( "Growing Pain" ); songs.add( "New Rules" ); System.out.println(songs.get( 0 )); // first element songs.remove(songs.size() - 1 ); // remove LAST element songs.add( "Blue Hour" ); Multiple choice How do you access the last element of an ArrayList a ? a.get(a.length) a.get(-1) a.get(a.size() - 1) a.get(a.size() - 1) . Indices run 0..size-1, so the last one is at size - 1 . (Java has no negative indexing, and Lists use size() , not length .) Multiple choice Why can't the internal array be declared T[] arr = new T[size] ? Because T is always an int. You can't create an array of a generic type in Java — so ArrayList uses Object[] (Object holds anything) and casts. Because arrays can't be resized. Slide 21: new T[size] is illegal. Since every type is-a Object , an Object[] can store any element, and you cast back to T on retrieval. Amortized time — the key ArrayList idea A single add is usually O(1), but the one add that triggers a resize costs O(n) (copy everything to the new array). Averaged over a long run of adds, the rare expensive copies spread out to amortized O(1) per add. T / F Amortized time is time taken averaged over a fixed, known sequence of operations — as opposed to random sampling from a distribution of operations. True False True (matches your quiz). Amortized = averaged over a known sequence (e.g. 1000 straight adds). Average = averaged over a random distribution of operations. They answer different questions. Multiple choice What are the worst-case and amortized time of an ArrayList add ? Both O(1) Worst case O(n) (the resize/copy), amortized O(1) Worst case O(1), amortized O(n) Slide 23–27: worst case is O(n) (when it must copy to a bigger array), but the amortized cost is O(1) because resizes are rare and their cost spreads over many cheap adds. Multiple choice When would you care about worst-case time rather than amortized? Real-time systems, where a guaranteed per-operation bound is critical. When you only ever do one operation. Never — amortized is always what matters. Slide 28: worst-case matters when guarantees are critical (real-time systems); amortized is fine when average performance is acceptable.

title: Lesson 9 · LinkedList — chained nodes
text: Lesson 9 · LinkedList — chained nodes A LinkedList stores each element in its own node allocated separately on the heap (non-contiguous memory). Each node holds its value and a reference to the next node . The list keeps a reference to the first node ( _head ), often the last ( _tail ), and the _size . Fill in — the LinkedList fields The LinkedList class has two reference-type fields: (which is required) and (which is optional). Check both Answers: _head and _tail — with the leading underscore (that's the field-naming convention, and what the quiz wanted; plain "head"/"tail" was marked wrong). _head is required to find the list at all; _tail is optional but makes adding at the end O(1). The Node From linkedList/NodeImpl.java — a value plus a pointer to the next node: public class NodeImpl <T> implements Node <T> { private T _value; private Node<T> _next; // reference to the NEXT node public NodeImpl (T value, Node<T> next) { _value = value; _next = next; } // getValue/setValue/getNext/setNext ... } T / F LinkedList nodes are stored in one contiguous block of memory, like an array. True False False (slide 47). Each node is allocated separately and can live anywhere on the heap; they're chained together by the _next references, not by being adjacent in memory. Multiple choice What is the time to access the i-th element L(i) of a LinkedList? O(1) — jump straight to it O(n) — you must walk from the head, following _next i times O(log n) — halve each step O(n) (slide 46). There's no direct indexing — to reach index i you start at _head and follow getNext() i times. This is the big trade-off vs an array's O(1) access. Singly vs Doubly linked Multiple choice What extra field does a doubly linked list's node have? A reference to the head A reference to the previous node (as well as next) Its index Slide 52: a doubly linked node adds a previous -node reference, so you can traverse in both directions (useful for, e.g., deleting a node when you only have a reference to it).

title: Lesson 9 · Code Writing
text: Lesson 9 · Code Writing Write each yourself, then reveal. These are the core LinkedList operations — the walking-with-a- current -pointer pattern shows up again and again. 1. The Node class Write a generic NodeImpl<T> with private _value and _next (a Node<T> ), a constructor taking both, and getters/setters for each. implements Node { ... }"> Show solution public class NodeImpl <T> implements Node <T> { private T _value; private Node<T> _next; public NodeImpl (T value, Node<T> next) { _value = value; _next = next; } public T getValue () { return _value; } public void setValue (T value) { _value = value; } public Node<T> getNext () { return _next; } public void setNext (Node<T> next) { _next = next; } } A node is basically a box with two things: the value and a reference to the next box. That _next reference is what chains the list together. 2. add at the tail Write add(T element) that appends a new node to the end. Fields available: _head , _tail , _size . Handle the empty-list case. Show solution public void add (T element) { Node<T> newNode = new NodeImpl <>(element, null ); if (isEmpty()) { // empty: new node is both head and tail _head = newNode; _tail = newNode; } else { // otherwise: link it after the current tail _tail.setNext(newNode); _tail = newNode; } _size++; } Keeping a _tail reference is what makes this O(1): you jump straight to the end. Without _tail you'd have to walk the whole list first — O(n). 3. get(index) — the traversal pattern Write get(int index) returning the value at that position (assume the index is valid). Show solution public T get ( int index) { Node<T> current = _head; // start at the head int i = 0 ; while (i < index) { // hop forward index times current = current.getNext(); i++; } return current.getValue(); } This walk-from-the-head-with-a- current -pointer is the LinkedList pattern, and it's exactly why get is O(n): reaching index i takes i hops. 4. reverse the list Write reverse() that reverses the node order in place (e.g. 10 -> 9 -> 8 becomes 8 -> 9 -> 10 ). Show solution public void reverse () { Node<T> prev = null ; Node<T> current = _head; _tail = _head; // old head becomes the new tail while (current != null ) { Node<T> nextNode = current.getNext(); // save the next current.setNext(prev); // flip this node's pointer backward prev = current; // advance prev current = nextNode; // advance current } _head = prev; // last node is the new head } The trick is the three pointers: prev , current , and a saved nextNode (so you don't lose the rest of the list when you flip current 's pointer). Walk through once, flipping each _next to point backward. 5. size() and isEmpty() Given a _size field, write both. Show solution public int size () { return _size; } public boolean isEmpty () { return _size == 0 ; } Because the list tracks _size as a field (updated on every add/remove), both are O(1) — no need to walk the list to count.

title: Practice · Time Complexity (easy → exam-level)
text: Practice · Time Complexity (easy → exam-level) For each snippet, give its Big-O in terms of n (or n and k ). Remember: sequential statements add (keep the largest); nested loops multiply ; a loop with a constant bound doesn't add an order. 1. Warm-up — single loop for ( int i= 0 ; i<n; i++) { sum += a[i]; } Multiple choice Big-O? O(1) O(n) O(n²) O(log n) O(n) . One loop of n iterations × O(1) body = O(n). 2. Two separate loops for ( int i= 0 ; i<n; i++) sum += a[i]; for ( int j= 0 ; j<n; j++) prod *= a[j]; Multiple choice Big-O? O(n²) O(n) O(2n) — you keep the 2 O(1) O(n) . The loops are sequential , not nested → you add : O(n) + O(n) = O(2n) = O(n). Drop the coefficient. (Nesting would multiply; running one after the other doesn't.) 3. No loop int x = a[ 0 ] + a[n- 1 ]; return x * 2 ; Multiple choice Big-O? O(1) O(n) O(2) O(log n) O(1) . A fixed number of operations regardless of n — array indexing and arithmetic are all constant time. 4. Nested loops for ( int i= 0 ; i<n; i++) for ( int j= 0 ; j<n; j++) grid[i][j] = i*j; Multiple choice Big-O? O(n) O(2n) O(n²) O(n log n) O(n²) . Nested loops multiply: n outer × n inner × O(1) body = O(n²). 5. Nested loop with a constant inner bound for ( int i= 0 ; i<n; i++) for ( int j= 0 ; j< 100 ; j++) // always 100 times total += grid[i][j]; Multiple choice Big-O? O(n) O(n²) O(100n²) O(1) O(n) . The inner loop runs a fixed 100 times — a constant, not tied to n. So it's n × 100 × O(1) = O(100n) = O(n). Watch for constant loop bounds! 6. Triangular nested loop for ( int i= 0 ; i<n; i++) for ( int j= 0 ; j<i; j++) // inner grows with i System.out.println(a[j]); Multiple choice Big-O? O(n) O(n²) O(n log n) O(log n) O(n²) . The inner loop runs 0+1+2+…+(n-1) = n(n-1)/2 total times ≈ ½n². Drop the constant ½ → O(n²). Even though each inner loop is short, they sum to a quadratic. 7. A loop that doubles the counter for ( int i= 1 ; i<n; i=i* 2 ) { // 1, 2, 4, 8, ... System.out.println(i); } Multiple choice Big-O? O(n) O(n²) O(1) O(log n) O(log n) . i doubles each pass, so it reaches n in about log₂ n steps. Anything that repeatedly multiplies/divides the counter (rather than adding) is logarithmic — same reason binary search is O(log n). 8. Exam-style — three loops, one with a fixed bound for ( int i= 0 ; i<n; i++) for ( int j=i; j<i+ 8 ; j++) // exactly 8 times for ( int k= 0 ; k<n; k++) x += i-j*k; Multiple choice Big-O? O(n³) O(n²) O(8n) O(n) O(n²) . Outer ≈ n, middle is a constant 8 , inner ≈ n → n × 8 × n = 8n² → O(n²). This is the exact trap from your L7 quiz: a middle loop with a constant bound does NOT make it cubic. 9. Two different arrays (lengths n and k) for ( int i= 0 ; i<n; i++) // a.length = n for ( int j= 0 ; j<k; j++) // b.length = k compare(a[i], b[j]); Multiple choice Big-O? O(n²) O(n) O(nk) O(n+k) O(nk) . When the two loop bounds are different variables , you keep both: n outer × k inner = O(nk). Don't collapse it to n² — that would only be right if k were also n. 10. Recursion — halving static void search ( int [] a, int lo, int hi, int key) { if (lo > hi) return ; int mid = (lo+hi)/ 2 ; if (a[mid]==key) return ; if (key < a[mid]) search (a, lo, mid- 1 , key); else search (a, mid+ 1 , hi, key); } Multiple choice Big-O? O(n) O(n²) O(2ⁿ) O(log n) O(log n) . This is binary search: each call throws away half the array and makes just one recursive call. Halving → log n levels, O(1) work each. 11. Recursion — double branching static int f ( int n) { if (n <= 1 ) return n; return f (n- 1 ) + f (n- 2 ); } Multiple choice Big-O? O(n) O(n log n) O(2ⁿ) O(log n) O(2ⁿ) . This is Fibonacci: two recursive calls per call, each barely smaller than n, so the call count roughly doubles each level → exponential. (Contrast with #10, which makes only one call and shrinks by half.)

text: Practice · Space Complexity Give the auxiliary space (extra memory the algorithm allocates, excluding the input ). A fixed set of variables → O(1). A new array/list sized by n → O(n). Recursion depth counts too: d levels deep → O(d) stack space. 1. A few counters int max = a[ 0 ], min = a[ 0 ]; for ( int i= 0 ; i<n; i++) { ... } Multiple choice Auxiliary space? O(1) O(n) O(n²) O(1) . Just a fixed handful of variables no matter how big n is. The input array doesn't count. 2. Building a copy int [] copy = new int [n]; for ( int i= 0 ; i<n; i++) copy[i] = a[i]* 2 ; Multiple choice Auxiliary space? O(1) O(n) O(n²) O(n) . new int[n] allocates memory that grows with the input size. A new array sized by n is the classic O(n)-space tell. 3. A 2-D table int [][] dp = new int [n][n]; Multiple choice Auxiliary space? O(1) O(n) O(n²) O(n²) . An n×n grid holds n² cells → quadratic space. 4. In-place swapping (bubble-sort inner logic) for ( int i= 0 ; i<n- 1 ; i++) if (a[i] > a[i+ 1 ]) { int t = a[i]; a[i]=a[i+ 1 ]; a[i+ 1 ]=t; } Multiple choice Auxiliary space? O(1) O(n) O(n²) O(1) . It rearranges the input array in place using only a single temp variable t — no new array. (This is why bubble sort is O(1) space even though it's O(n²) time.) 5. Fixed-size buffer, regardless of n int [] counts = new int [ 256 ]; // always 256 for ( int i= 0 ; i<n; i++) counts[a[i]]++; Multiple choice Auxiliary space? O(1) O(n) O(256n) O(1) . title: Practice · Code Writing — Recursion
text: Practice · Code Writing — Recursion For each, write the method yourself first, then reveal to compare. Every one needs a base case (stops the recursion) and a recursive case (moves toward it). 1. Sum 1..n Write int sumTo(int n) that returns 1 + 2 + … + n (assume n ≥ 0; sumTo(0) = 0). Show solution public static int sumTo ( int n) { if (n == 0 ) return 0 ; // base case return n + sumTo (n - 1 ); // recursive case } Each call peels off n and adds it to the sum of everything below it. Base case n==0 returns 0 so the additions can unwind. 2. Power Write int power(int base, int exp) that returns base^exp (assume exp ≥ 0; anything^0 = 1). Show solution public static int power ( int base, int exp) { if (exp == 0 ) return 1 ; // base case: x^0 = 1 return base * power (base, exp - 1 ); // one fewer multiply } Reduce the exponent toward 0 each call. power(2,3) = 2 * power(2,2) = 2*2*power(2,1) = 2*2*2*power(2,0) = 8. 3. Sum of an array Write int arraySum(int[] a, int i) returning the sum of a[i..end] . Call it as arraySum(a, 0) . Show solution public static int arraySum ( int [] a, int i) { if (i == a.length) return 0 ; // past the end → nothing to add return a[i] + arraySum (a, i + 1 ); // this element + the rest } The index i is what shrinks toward the base case. When i reaches a.length , there's nothing left, so return 0. 4. Reverse a string Write String reverse(String s) that returns s reversed (base case: empty or 1-char string). Show solution public static String reverse (String s) { if (s.length() <= 1 ) return s; // base case return reverse (s.substring( 1 )) + s.charAt( 0 ); } Peel off the first char, reverse the rest, then stick the first char on the end . reverse("cat") = reverse("at") + 'c' = "ta" + "c" = "tac". 5. Count down (and think about complexity) Write void countdown(int n) that prints n, n-1, …, 1 then stops. Then: what are its time and space complexity? Show solution public static void countdown ( int n) { if (n == 0 ) return ; // base case System.out.println(n); countdown (n - 1 ); // one call, n shrinks by 1 } Time O(n) — n calls, O(1) work each (linear recursion). Space O(n) — it goes n frames deep on the call stack before unwinding.

title: Practice · Code Writing — Classes & OOP
text: Practice · Code Writing — Classes & OOP Practice the anatomy: private fields, a constructor that sets them, and public methods (getters/setters) with validation. Fields use the class's leading-underscore convention. 1. Rectangle Write a Rectangle class with private _width and _height (doubles), a constructor, a getter for each, and an area() method. Show solution public class Rectangle { private double _width; private double _height; public Rectangle ( double width, double height) { _width = width; _height = height; } public double getWidth () { return _width; } public double getHeight () { return _height; } public double area () { return _width * _height; // derived property } } area() is a good example of a derived property — it's computed from fields rather than stored, so there's no _area field to keep in sync. 2. BankAccount with validation Write a BankAccount with a private _balance , a constructor taking a starting balance, getBalance() , a deposit(double amt) that ignores non-positive amounts, and a withdraw(double amt) that refuses to overdraw. Show solution public class BankAccount { private double _balance; public BankAccount ( double startingBalance) { _balance = startingBalance; } public double getBalance () { return _balance; } public void deposit ( double amt) { if (amt <= 0 ) return ; // validate: ignore bad input _balance += amt; } public void withdraw ( double amt) { if (amt <= 0 || amt > _balance) return ; // no overdraw _balance -= amt; } } The private field + validating methods are encapsulation in action: no outside code can set a negative balance, because the only doors in ( deposit / withdraw ) check first. 3. Student with a validating setter Write a Student with private _name (String) and _gpa (double). Constructor sets the name; provide getGpa() and setGpa(double gpa) that only accepts values in 0.0–4.0. Show solution public class Student { private String _name; private double _gpa; public Student (String name) { _name = name; _gpa = 0.0 ; } public double getGpa () { return _gpa; } public void setGpa ( double gpa) { if (gpa < 0.0 || gpa > 4.0 ) return ; // reject out-of-range _gpa = gpa; } } A read-only-ish field with a guarded setter: the object can never hold a GPA outside 0–4, because that rule lives inside setGpa .

title: Practice · Code Writing — Interfaces & Tests
text: Practice · Code Writing — Interfaces & Tests An interface lists method signatures (no bodies); an implementing class provides the bodies as public methods. JUnit tests use @BeforeEach to set up and @Test methods with assertions. 1. Write an interface Write an interface Shape that requires two methods: double area() and double perimeter() . Show solution public interface Shape { double area (); double perimeter (); } Signatures only — each ends in a semicolon, no { } , no fields. It's a contract, not an implementation. 2. Implement the interface Write a Circle class that implements Shape : private _radius , a constructor, and both required methods ( area = πr² , perimeter = 2πr ). Use Math.PI . Show solution public class Circle implements Shape { private double _radius; public Circle ( double radius) { _radius = radius; } public double area () { return Math.PI * _radius * _radius; } public double perimeter () { return 2 * Math.PI * _radius; } } Because it keeps the Shape promise, a Circle is a Shape — so Shape s = new Circle(3); is legal. Both interface methods must be declared public . 3. Write JUnit tests Write a test class CircleTest that, before each test, creates a Circle of radius 2, then tests that area() is about 12.566 (use a delta) and that the circle object is not null. Show solution import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test; import org.junit.jupiter.api.BeforeEach; import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*; public class CircleTest { private Circle c; @BeforeEach public void setup () { c = new Circle ( 2.0 ); } @Test public void testArea () { assertEquals( 12.566 , c.area(), 0.001 ); // delta for doubles } @Test public void testNotNull () { assertNotNull(c); } } The delta 0.001 matters: area() is a double, so you can't check exact equality. assertEquals(expected, actual, delta) passes if they're within the delta.

Output: 1600 (checkClock's local time). Note each method has its own local time ; passing time copies the value into hour . Q2 · The 5 components of a class, top to bottom (2 pts) Show answer Instance Field → Class Field → Constructor → Instance Method → Class Method. Q3 · Fill What is the universal reference type? Check Object — every reference type is a subclass of Object. Q4 · Fill What is the universal reference value? Check null — any reference variable can hold null. Q7 · An object has an is-a relationship with (can be typed as) which 3 things? (2 pts) Show answer Its class, any interfaces its class implements, and its class' superclasses. Q11 · MC Worst-case time complexity of quick sort? O(n) O(n log n) O(n²) O(n²) — presorted input with a bad pivot gives maximally unbalanced partitions. Q12 · Time complexity of the method in terms of n and x (3 pts) if (n % 2 == 0) { for (i = 0; i < n; i++) // O(n) for (j = i; j > 0; j--) // O(n) counter++; // → O(n²) } else { for (k = x; k < x*3; k++) // O(x³ region) for (m = ...; ...; m++) // O(x²) counter++; // → O(x⁵) } Show answer O(n² + x⁵). text: Quiz 4 — BuildHeap, AVL, Red-Black, Hashing (L12–L17) Q1 · Basic pseudocode for BuildHeap (5 pts) — may call bubbleDown Show answer public static void buildHeap (List<Integer> list) { // start at the last parent, go up to the root for ( int i = list.size()/ 2 - 1 ; i >= 0 ; i--) { bubbleDown(i); } } Bottom-up: heapify from the last parent index down to 0, sifting each node down. This is O(n). Q2–3 use this AVL tree: root 14; left 8 (child 3); right 33 (left 18→right 22, right 67→children 48, 70). Q2 · Fill If you insert 20, at which node does the first imbalance appear? (write "none" if balanced) Check 18. 20 becomes the left child of 22 (right child of 18); node 18 becomes unbalanced (an RL case). Q3 · Draw the resulting tree after 40 is inserted (3 pts) Show answer Insert 40 → left of 48. Node 14 becomes -2 (right-heavy, RR case) → rotate left at 14. Result: 33 / \\ 14 67 / \\ / \\ 8 18 48 70 / \\ / 3 22 40 (Confirmed by the graded rubric.) Only one rotation — a single left rotation at the root 14 — restores balance; 33 becomes the new root. Q4–6 use a red-black tree: root 16(B); 10, 30; 5, 14, 22, 90; 90→57, 98; 57→42, 60. Q4 · Fill What is the black height of the tree? Check 2 (accepted: 2 or 3 depending on whether you count the root/NIL). Black height = number of black nodes on a root-to-NIL path, not counting the start. Q5 · Fill Black height of node 30 (not including node 30)? Check 1 (accepted: 1 or 2). Q6 · Draw the resulting tree after 16 is deleted (4 pts) Show answer Delete root 16 → replace with in-order successor 22, then repair red-black invariants (recolor / rotate to resolve any double-black). The result is a valid red-black tree rooted at 22 with 10 (children 5, 14) on the left and the 30/90/57/98/42/60 structure rebalanced on the right. This is a full RB-deletion drawing problem — practice it with the animated deletion walkthrough in Lesson 14 . Q7 · T/F Red-black trees are used more commonly than AVL trees because they are faster. True False True (per this course) — red-black trees rebalance with fewer rotations , making insert/delete faster, so they're the common default (e.g. TreeMap). Nuance: AVL trees are actually faster for search because they're more tightly balanced. Q8 · Chaining hash table, insert at head. h(k)=k mod 7; insert 1, 5, 12, 8, 15 (3 pts) Show answer index 0: (empty) index 1: 15 → 8 → 1 index 2: (empty) index 3: (empty) index 4: (empty) index 5: 12 → 5 index 6: (empty) 1→1, 5→5, 12→5 (collision, prepend), 8→1, 15→1. Head insertion puts the newest at the front of each chain. Q9 · Fill Load factor of that table? Check 5/7 (N = 5 elements, M = 7 slots). Double hashing gives each key its own step size, avoiding clustering. Q11 · Fill Load factor of that table? Check 5/7 . (Probing, by contrast, caps load at ≤ 1.) Q14 · Complexity table — fill in amortized (left) / worst case (right) (9 pts) Type each Big-O from memory (e.g. O(1) , O(log n) , O(n) ). Spelling of spaces doesn't matter. Heaps (resizing) amort / worst Balanced BSTs amort / worst Hash Tables (resizing) amort / worst Insert / / / Search / / / Delete (min) / / / Check all Reveal answers Clear Explain the reasoning Heaps (resizing). Insert = add at the end + sift up along the height → O(log n) ; the worst case O(n) happens only when the backing array is full and must be resized (copy all n elements) — but that resize is rare, so it amortizes back to O(log n) . Search (for an arbitrary value) is O(n) either way — a heap only orders parent-vs-child, not left-vs-right, so there's no way to prune; you may scan every node. Delete-min = remove the root, move the last element up, sift down → O(log n) , with the same O(n) resize worst case. Balanced BSTs (AVL / Red-Black). Every operation follows a single root-to-leaf path, and the balancing keeps the height at O(log n). There's no array to resize , so amortized and worst case are both O(log n) for insert, search, and delete. Hash tables (resizing). With a good hash function and a bounded load factor, each bucket holds ~a constant number of items, so insert/search/delete are O(1) amortized . The worst case is O(n) — either every key collides into one bucket/cluster, or an insert triggers a resize that rehashes all n elements. Because resizing only happens occasionally (doubling), it amortizes away to O(1). The pattern: the two resizing structures (heap, hash table) show a gap between amortized and worst case because of the rare O(n) resize; the balanced BST needs no resizing, so its two columns match.

Both O(n log n) buildHeap O(n); n inserts O(n log n) buildHeap O(n log n); n inserts O(n) buildHeap is O(n) (bottom-up); doing n independent inserts is O(n log n) .
